name: Caffeine shampoo

lead: Caffeine shampoos are cosmetic products sold to people with thinning hair, with Alpecin the best-known brand. They are an easy add-on to a hair-loss routine, aimed at slower thinning and fuller hair.

The idea is that caffeine absorbed at the follicles counters the effects of androgens on hair. Caffeine-based products are described as promising in lab and animal work, and one 2020 study examined a phyto-caffeine shampoo in women with female androgenetic alopecia; its results were not available in the sources reviewed.

paras: It is used in place of a regular shampoo, left on the scalp briefly during washing, and typically combined with other hair-loss treatments. Users keep it up over months.
No safety information was available in the sources reviewed. These are sold as cosmetic products rather than approved hair-loss drugs, so they carry no drug-style claims.

angle.text: Caffeine shampoos such as Alpecin are marketed to people with thinning hair as an easy addition to a hair-loss routine. Caffeine at the follicles is meant to counter androgen effects, slowing thinning for fuller hair. One study has looked at a caffeine shampoo in women.

lead: Caffeine shampoo is a rinse-off cosmetic shampoo that contains caffeine and is marketed to people with thinning hair, aiming to keep more hair on the head and make hair look and feel thicker. The best-known brand is Alpecin, a German shampoo line for men whose maker says its caffeine content can help reduce hair loss [1]. The idea is that caffeine applied to the scalp may work against the effects of androgens on hair follicles, and users wash with it as part of a routine alongside treatments such as minoxidil or finasteride [2][3].

A 2020 study in the Giornale Italiano di Dermatologia e Venereologia tested a cosmetic phyto-caffeine shampoo in women with androgenetic alopecia in a single-centre, double-blind, randomised, parallel trial against a control shampoo over six months. The phyto-caffeine group had significantly fewer hairs pulled in a hair-pull test than the control group (-3.1 versus -0.5 hairs), improved on hair loss intensity and hair strength, and both products were well tolerated [4]. A 2019 review in the International Journal of Cosmetic Science described caffeine as the most studied phytochemical for hair loss and said the studies offer reasonable evidence that, when dosed adequately for long enough, caffeine reaches the follicle at levels that could ameliorate hair loss in some patients [1].

In March 2018 the UK Advertising Standards Authority ruled that Alpecin could no longer say in UK ads that it helps reduce hair loss, finding the evidence the company had submitted (eight full studies, several summaries and a consumer survey) inadequate [1].
infobox: ASA, March 2018: 'helps reduce hair loss' claim not allowed

paras: Caffeine shampoos are rinse-off scalp products with caffeine as an active cosmetic ingredient. The 2020 trial abstract describes androgenetic alopecia as the most common type of hair loss in both sexes, affecting up to 57 percent of women by age 80, and as carrying a heavy psychological burden, which it gives as background for testing caffeine-based products [4].

Alpecin is a German shampoo brand for men, said by Wikipedia to have been established in 1905 (its infobox gives 1930 as the introduction date) [1]. It has sponsored professional cycling teams, including Team Giant-Alpecin from 2015, Katusha-Alpecin from 2017 to 2019 and Alpecin-Fenix from 2020 [1].

The manufacturer publishes its supporting studies on its website while noting it cannot guarantee their accuracy [1]. The 2018 UK ASA ruling concluded that the claim that Alpecin helps reduce hair loss was misleading for lack of adequate scientific evidence [1].

On T Nation, users describe caffeine shampoo as an add-on: one poster says using Nizoral and Alpecin together made hair look and feel thicker within a week [5]; another says a caffeine shampoo is the only thing they use against hair loss while considering an oral steroid [6]. A poster discussing compounds for facial hair says hair-loss shampoos with biotin and caffeine seemed to make their beard and body hair hairier but did nothing for actual thinning [7]. Posts discussing hair loss regimens typically place shampoos alongside the so-called big three of minoxidil, finasteride and ketoconazole [2]. A Hacker News item also links a podcast asking whether caffeine hair products like Alpecin stimulate hair growth [8].

The 2020 randomised trial in female androgenetic alopecia reported significantly fewer hairs pulled with the phyto-caffeine shampoo than control at six months, with improvements on most secondary measures and good tolerability [4]. The 2019 International Journal of Cosmetic Science review discussed the follicle-level evidence for caffeine [1]. No men-specific trial of a caffeine shampoo was found.

lore.intro: Forum users mention caffeine shampoo as a low-effort adjunct to minoxidil and finasteride and to hormone-therapy hair-loss worries [5][6][2].
